title: Daily Health Briefing
intro: Good morning! Here's today's research digest across your tracked topics, pulled from recent, reputable sources (PubMed, JAMA, NIH/PMC, NEJM, AASM, and peer-reviewed journals). Citations are linked as chips below each section. This is informational only — not medical advice; discuss anything actionable with your clinician.

sections.body:
The longevity field is entering a phase of **larger, better-powered human trials** — a shift from the small proof-of-concept studies that dominated the last few years.

- **Rapamycin** remains the most-watched geroprotector, and the pipeline is expanding well beyond the completed **PEARL** trial (where 48 weeks of low-dose weekly rapamycin was *safe* and improved **lean tissue mass and pain in women**, but missed its visceral-fat primary endpoint). A 2026 *GeroScience* review catalogs three notable new trials: **RESTOR** (NCT06658093) — a dose-finding PK/PD study of rapamycin *and* everolimus in adults 65–90; an **ARPA-H PROSPR** phase 3 ($38M, ~726 adults aged 60–65 at UT Health San Antonio) testing daily rapamycin and two other candidates for one year; and a University of Arizona 3-year trial in adults 65+ using **physical function and transition to frailty** (plus IL-6) as endpoints.
- Importantly, PEARL's compounded rapamycin had only ~1/3 the bioavailability of commercial rapamycin, which likely blunted its results — so newer trials testing a **wider dose range** matter.
- Beyond rapalogs, a 2026 review notes **mesenchymal stem-cell preparations** now lead the regenerative-aging space, with three positive RCTs targeting **skeletal-muscle frailty**.

Practical framing: the honest state of the science is that **no supplement or drug has been shown to extend human lifespan.** Favor interventions being tested in real RCTs, be skeptical of single-supplement "longevity" marketing, and treat off-label rapamycin as experimental (no standardized dosing or long-term safety data in healthy people).

sections.body:
This week's evidence sharpens *what HIIT is good for* — and, for the first time, weighs it head-to-head against steady-state cardio in a common women's-health condition.

- A **2026 systematic review & meta-analysis** (19 RCTs in middle-aged and older women) found HIIT **significantly improves VO₂max** vs. controls (SMD = 1.20, 95% CI 0.86–1.54) with **high certainty** of evidence — consistent across age, body-mass status, and program length. Walking ability improved borderline-significantly.
- The same review found **no significant gain in muscle strength, flexibility, or sit-to-stand** from HIIT alone. The authors' conclusion is blunt: *HIIT alone is insufficient to comprehensively improve functional performance* — pair it with **resistance and balance training**.
- New for **PCOS** (the most common endocrine disorder in reproductive-age women): a 2026 meta-analysis of supervised RCTs (≥12 weeks) found **no statistically significant superiority of HIIT over moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT)** for weight, cardiorespiratory, metabolic, or hormonal outcomes — so either can be chosen based on **preference and adherence** (evidence certainty is low, so bigger trials are needed).
- A broader women's-fitness meta-analysis echoes this: HIIT and continuous training raise VO₂max about equally, and **more sessions = bigger gains** in both formats.

Bottom line: use HIIT for time-efficient cardio, but the best program is **multimodal** — intervals for the heart, resistance work for strength/lean mass, and consistency above all.

sources.title: Effects of HIIT on cardiopulmonary fitness and physical function in middle-aged and elderly women: systematic review & meta-analysis

sections.body:
**Pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT)** stays the evidence-based **first-line** treatment for stress urinary incontinence (SUI), and this week's trials focus on *how to make it work better* — supervision, timing, and add-ons.

- **Supervision matters.** A 2026 RCT (60 women) directly comparing **supervised vs. unsupervised home** PFMT found supervised training far more effective: pad-test leakage fell from 22.9 g → 3.2 g (p < 0.001) vs. a non-significant drop in the home group, and **66.7% reached Oxford grade 4–5** strength vs. 13.3%. Unsupervised PFMT is still a reasonable fallback when access is limited **and** adherence is good.
- **Timing matters.** A 2026 RCT (90 women) of **intensive preoperative PFMT** before mid-urethral sling surgery showed significant gains in muscle strength (Modified Oxford, d = 0.85) and incontinence severity (d = 0.90) — and **43% postponed their planned surgery** afterward, supporting PFMT as a low-risk step before opting for an operation.
- **Add-ons for specific groups.** In postmenopausal women (who often have low local androgen), a double-blind RCT found **vaginal androgen cream + PFMT** beat placebo cream + PFMT on daily pad use, 24-hour pad test, and ICIQ-UI-SF scores at 3 and 6 months, with no severe adverse events — an early but promising adjunct.

Key point: **correct technique and consistency beat sheer reps.** Confirm activation with a clinician or biofeedback, and choose supervised programs when you can.

sources.title: Managing female SUI: an RCT evaluating supervised vs. unsupervised pelvic floor muscle training

sections.body:
The freshest and most significant news for **p53-mutated** cancers is a genuine milestone in what was long considered an "undruggable" target — plus a sober reminder of why **HER2+/TP53 co-mutation** is so aggressive.

- **First-in-human p53 reactivation reaches NEJM.** In **February 2026**, results from the phase 1 portion of the **PYNNACLE** trial (NCT04585750) of **rezatapopt (PC14586)** — a small molecule that selectively **restores wild-type function to the TP53 Y220C mutant** — were published in the *New England Journal of Medicine*. It's the first clinical demonstration of selective mutant-p53 reactivation. The registrational **phase 2** basket (~114 patients, KRAS wild-type) includes a dedicated **breast-cancer cohort**; interim data reported a **~17% objective response rate (2/12)** in breast cancer, with much higher activity in ovarian cancer (~46%). The FDA granted rezatapopt **Fast Track** designation.
- **Why HER2+/TP53 is high-risk.** A 2024 SABCS ctDNA analysis in HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer found that **TP53 + PIK3CA co-mutations** track with **poorer 10-year survival, shorter PFS, worse response to trastuzumab**, and more visceral spread — useful for anticipating resistance and tailoring lines of therapy.
- **A p53-informed chemo strategy.** The ongoing **p53 Breast Cancer Trial** (NCT02965950) stratifies patients by TP53 status and tests **dose-dense cyclophosphamide**, with an arm (Arm C) for **first-line HER2-positive metastatic** disease.

Important framing: rezatapopt only targets the specific **Y220C** mutation (not all p53 mutations), and most of this is **investigational**. "Alternative" here should mean *evidence-based, trial-based options discussed with an oncologist* — a complement to, not a replacement for, standard HER2-directed care.

sections.body:
New 2026 evidence keeps pointing the same direction for restless or disjointed sleep: **behavioral therapy first, medication and supplements as limited add-ons.**

- A **2026 AASM meta-analysis of 15 RCTs** (Buysse et al.) found a striking asymmetry in *combination* treatment: **adding CBT-I to an existing sleep medication** produces clinically meaningful gains, but **adding medication to CBT-I** does *not* — none of the sleep outcomes (severity, sleep efficiency, onset latency, wake-after-sleep-onset) cleared a meaningful threshold, and daytime **depression scores may even worsen**. So if you're starting fresh, **CBT-I alone is the better default**.
- A 2026 evidence review (28 high-quality sources; *Frontiers in Psychiatry*) reaffirms **multicomponent CBT-I** — sleep restriction, stimulus control, cognitive restructuring, relaxation — as first-line, with **4–8 sessions over 6–8 weeks** and **digital/telehealth delivery working as well as in-person**. Five international guidelines agree; **sleep hygiene alone is not** sufficient as a standalone treatment.
- Can't access CBT-I? A 2026 network meta-analysis ranked **Meditative Movement Therapy** (tai chi, qigong, yoga) as the strongest *adjunct/alternative* (PSQI MD −5.50), with **acupuncture** also showing consistent benefit.
- **Supplements:** AASM continues to **suggest against melatonin** for chronic insomnia (best reserved for circadian issues like jet lag/shift work). **Magnesium L-threonate** has early promising data for sleep quality, but evidence overall remains limited.

Best-practice habits for disjointed sleep:

1. Hold a **fixed wake time**, even on weekends.
2. Use the bed **only for sleep**; keep the room cool, dark, and quiet.
3. Dim lights and cut screens during a wind-down window.
4. If it persists beyond a few weeks, see a provider to rule out **sleep apnea** and pursue **CBT-I**.
